To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people who are idealistic and absolutists are more likely to feel that their intentions are praiseworthy than the consequences of their behavior, whereas people who are relativistic and situationists are more likely feel that their behavior is praiseworthy if it generates good consequences than if they have the right intentions.

the moral evaluation of one’s own behavior is influenced by the moral orientation of the individual, the nature of the action (whether it is for oneself or for others), the consequences of the behavior, and the interaction of the first two factors with the third.

(1) idealistic individuals who emphasize the importance of moral principles are more likely to feel positively about their moral self when working for a good cause, even when they fail; (2) relativistic individuals are less likely to feel positively when working for charity, irrespective of whether they succeed or fail; and (3) principled individuals who emphasize the need to make the best choice in each situation are more likely to report feeling positively when working for themselves, even when they succeed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the moral self, the psychological representation that we have of our own morality.
the moral evaluation of one’s own actions, and the role of motives and outcomes in this process.
how individuals make moral self-evaluations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the absolutist is the one who is more likely to be motivated by the desire of doing what is morally right and is more likely to feel good about himself when he does what is morally right, even when the outcome of his action is not the best possible one.
the impact of motives and outcome on moral self-evaluation depends on the individual’s moral orientation.
the moral self is a complex entity that reflects both the intentions and the consequences of one's actions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people are motivated to act morally and they do so when it is in their self-interest.

the more idealistic an individual, the more likely they are to be motivated by moral principles, and the more likely they will be to feel morally virtuous when working for the greater good, irrespective of their success or failure.
the more idealistic the individual, the greater the emphasis on moral principles and intentions, and the less the importance of outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
moral philosophy theory can be used to make testable predictions about how individuals will evaluate themselves and their behavior.
the moral self is a dynamic construct and not just a reflection of one's moral philosophy.
the way in which individuals think about their own moral actions has implications for their well-being.
